source.title_on_document: How LLMs Distort Our Written Language

supplement.where: Integrated Appendix, pp. 21-95. Actual appendix section lettering differs from the contents page: the statistical table is section E (p. 46), and essay examples run through section I (pp. 61-95). No separate external statistical supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: User-study instructions, questionnaires and demographics (pp. 22-26); revision prompts and robustness plots (pp. 26-43); judge prompts (pp. 44-46); Table 1 with peer-review category proportions, z-scores and p-values (p. 46); example essays and interactions (pp. 47-95). No numerical diversity effect or corresponding standard error is supplied for the main essay study or ArgRewrite-v2.

paper_design_summary: Prolific participants were randomly assigned to write an argumentative essay with or without an embedded LLM, but reported semantic-diversity comparisons distinguish heavy and light users within the AI-access arm rather than comparing the two full randomized arms. A second study compares existing human revisions from ArgRewrite-v2 with researcher-generated LLM revisions, and a third compares scientific-review content classified as human or AI generated. The main writing study scores essay embeddings and collects self-reports; a separately mentioned preliminary pilot only informs the usage-classification rule.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were randomized to no LLM access or access to embedded gpt-4o-mini while writing. The AI-access arm was subsequently classified by actual usage into LLM-Influenced and LLM groups; those usage groups were not randomly assigned. The authors say the classification rule was determined a priori, before analysis, following a pilot (p. 5, section 3.1).
assignment.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions:
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 3.1, Human Study; p. 5, section 3.1, usage classification

arms.name: Human User (no LLM access)
arms.description: Randomized control; no LLM, AI assistant, or internet during essay writing (p. 4, section 3.1; p. 22, section A.4). The printed allocation count is not separately identified as the outcome-specific analyzed count.

arms.name: AI-assisted (all assigned access)
arms.description: Randomized access to embedded gpt-4o-mini, used freely while writing (p. 4, section 3.1). Contains both usage subgroups below; these are not additional independent arms. Outcome-specific analyzed count is not separately given.

arms.name: LLM-Influenced (AI-access subgroup)
arms.description: Observed usage subgroup: self-reported less than 40% LLM-generated text, checked against interaction transcripts; 28 out of 55 are explicitly classified here (p. 5, section 3.1). Nested within the AI-access arm. AI remained available even for nonusers.

arms.name: LLM (heavy-use AI-access subgroup)
arms.description: Observed extensive generative-use subgroup, nested within the AI-access arm (p. 5, section 3.1). No explicit subgroup count is printed; no count is calculated by subtracting other groups.

participants.exclusions: The paper repeatedly describes the main study as n = 100 (pp. 4-5, section 3.1), and Figure 12 refers to 100 users (p. 26). This is the reported overall study sample, not a verified complete-case count for every outcome. Actual exclusions, attrition, and outcome-specific denominators are not stated. Control instructions threaten nonpayment for detected AI use but do not report any resulting exclusions (p. 22, section A.4). Arm counts 45 and 55 are explicitly given in the assignment paragraph; separate analyzed counts for these full arms are left null. No intention-to-treat analysis is claimed here.
participants.who: Native English speakers recruited through Prolific; the reported sample includes students and nonstudents (p. 4, section 3.1; p. 26, Figure 12).
participants.quote: We conducted a human user study of 100 participants
participants.locator: pp. 4-5, section 3.1, Human Study; p. 22, section A.1; p. 26, Figure 12

ai_tool.how_used: Embedded chatbot freely available during essay production; interaction history and final essay recorded (p. 4, section 3.1). Users could seek ideas, information or feedback, revise text, or generate essay text. The usage-based split is described on p. 5; 12 out of 55 refused to use the LLM to generate their essay at all. gpt-4o, mentioned on p. 7, was an analysis judge, not the participant assistance model.

task.description: Write an argumentative essay answering Does money lead to happiness? (p. 4, section 3.1). This writing task is within scope through comparison of semantic similarity across writers, rather than an externally rated creativity score.
task.duration: Estimated 35 minutes for the entire study, maximum 1 hour; writing-only duration is not separately stated (p. 22, section A.1).

outcomes.name: Across-writer semantic dispersion / clustering of final essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each final essay is encoded with MiniLM-L6-v2 and projected into two dimensions by t-SNE. Diversity is assessed visually from the spread and clustering of essays in Figure 4b and described in section 4.2. No scalar diversity index, arm mean or SD, numerical arm difference, or uncertainty for diversity is reported. Each point represents an essay, not an independent pairwise similarity estimate. The comparison uses actual-usage subgroups within the randomized AI-access arm, not the full randomized contrast.

contrasts.reported: Figure-only result: heavy-use essays form a distinct tight cluster, while control essays occupy a broad region. The paper interprets this as homogenization. No numerical diversity effect or test is printed. This is an observed usage-subgroup comparison, not a randomized heavy-use effect.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Figure 4b and section 4.2; p. 9, section 4.2

contrasts.reported: The paper describes LLM-influenced essays as occupying a similar semantic distribution to control essays. Figure-only comparison; no equivalence test or numerical diversity statistic is reported. Subgroup membership was based on usage, not randomization.

diversity_detail.metric: Visual spread and clustering of essay embeddings after t-SNE; no numerical diversity index.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Final essays across writers, displayed together and marked by no-access control, LLM-Influenced, and heavy-use LLM group. No all-pairs or centroid-based scalar summary is specified.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported for the diversity result; no SE, confidence interval, participant-level test, bootstrap, or permutation analysis. The t-tests in Figure 4a concern self-reports and must not be attached to Figure 4b.
diversity_detail.notes: Direction is coded for diversity: the tighter heavy-use cluster means lower diversity. The reported N = 100 is a study-level people count; the exact number of plotted/usable essays is not independently stated. The original two randomized arms have no reported numerical diversity contrast. No AI-withdrawal task was administered.

studies.label: ArgRewrite-v2 human versus LLM essay revisions

assignment.what_was_assigned: Researchers generated LLM revisions of existing human D1 drafts and compared them with the original human D2 revisions. Original students received human feedback; no person was assigned AI assistance. Comparisons are matched on the original essay, with model, prompt, and expert-feedback variants (pp. 5-6, section 3.1).
assignment.quote: We compare the LLM-generated D2 drafts with the human-written D2,

arms.name: Human D1 (original draft reference)
arms.description: Original unassisted essays from the same source students; reference locations for revision arrows, not a separate sample (pp. 5-7, sections 3.1-3.2).

arms.name: Human D2 (human-revised baseline)
arms.description: The same students revised their own original essays following expert human feedback; no AI assistance (pp. 5-6, section 3.1).

arms.name: LLM-generated D2 revisions
arms.description: Researchers prompted gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, and claude-haiku to revise the existing D1 essays under general, minimal, grammar, completion, and expansion prompts, with/without expert feedback variants. This arm contains generated outputs, not additional human participants (p. 6, section 3.1; pp. 26-34, sections B.1-B.4).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions are reported in this paper. The 86 people are the original university-student authors whose 86 source essays are reused, not newly recruited AI-assisted writers. Human D1 and D2 refer to the same people; generated revisions do not add people (p. 5, section 3.1; p. 7, section 3.2).
participants.who: University students in the existing ArgRewrite-v2 corpus, collected in 2021 and released in 2022 before ChatGPT (p. 5, section 3.1). Country is not stated in this document.
participants.quote: ArgRewrite-v2 (Kashefi et al., 2022) is a dataset of argumentative writing revisions collected from 86 university students.
participants.locator: p. 5, section 3.1, ArgRewrite-v2; p. 7, section 3.2, 86 different essays

ai_tool.name_model: gpt-5-mini; gemini-2.5-flash; claude-haiku (Claude version inconsistent within the PDF)
ai_tool.how_used: Automated researcher-generated edits of preexisting essays, not live assistance to their authors. Prompts cover general, minimal, grammar, completion, and expansion revisions, with and without original expert feedback (p. 6, section 3.1; p. 26, section B.1; pp. 26-34, sections B.2-B.4). Figure 25 calls the Claude model Claude-3.5-Haiku (p. 34), whereas the examples identify Claude Haiku 4.5 (p. 61, section I); no version is silently substituted.

task.description: Original students wrote and revised an argumentative op-ed for or against self-driving cars. LLMs were subsequently prompted to revise the same original drafts (pp. 5-6, section 3.1).

outcomes.name: Semantic convergence across human versus LLM revisions
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: D1 and D2 essay embeddings are projected by PCA; arrows show direction and magnitude of semantic changes. The authors interpret aligned LLM changes and reduced spread as homogenization, compared with more varied human revision directions. MiniLM-L6-v2 and gemini-004 embeddings, the different models, the editing prompts, and with/without expert feedback plots are robustness variants of this same outcome (p. 1, Figure 1; p. 9, Figure 5 and section 4.2; pp. 26-34, Figures 13-25). This is AI-generated output versus historical human output, not an AI-assistance effect in people.
outcomes.delay: No AI exposure/withdrawal or human follow-up design. Historical human essays were collected in 2021; LLM revisions were generated later, with no experimental delay stated (p. 5, section 3.1).

contrasts.reported: Figure-only semantic result: human revisions make smaller, more varied shifts, whereas LLM revisions shift in a common direction and are described as less diverse. General revisions show the largest semantic shift for gpt-5-mini and the smallest for claude-haiku; completion/expansion prompts produce larger shifts than lighter-edit prompts. No numerical diversity effect, SD, SE, CI, or diversity test is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 1, Figure 1; p. 9, Figure 5 and section 4.2; pp. 26-34, sections B.2-B.4, Figures 13-25

diversity_detail.metric: PCA visualization of semantic displacement and convergence; no scalar dispersion, pairwise-similarity, or diversity statistic is reported.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: MiniLM-L6-v2 (p. 1, Figure 1; p. 29, section B.3); gemini-004 (p. 9, Figure 5). Appendix captions on pp. 29-31 instead spell the MiniLM model MiniLM-L6-004.
diversity_detail.computed_over: The source essays and their matched D1-to-D2 revisions across student authors, compared by human versus LLM source and by model/prompt/feedback setting. n_units = 86 denotes source essays (p. 7, section 3.2), not the number of generated drafts across all settings.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No uncertainty estimate or statistical test for semantic convergence is reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Lower diversity is the authors' interpretation of the plotted convergence. Magnitude of change from an individual original draft alone is not an across-person diversity measure. Human writers never received the generated revisions as assistance; question is none, and mixed availability distinguishes human output without AI from AI-generated output. Immediate is only a form timing label for the displayed drafts, not evidence of an immediate human treatment effect.

studies.label: Observational analysis of ICLR 2026 peer reviews

assignment.what_was_assigned: Existing reviews were classified using Pangram AI detection, then human-written and LLM-generated reviews were selected for the same conference papers. AI use was not assigned or directly observed (p. 6, section 3.1).
assignment.quote: We selected only those papers with one review written entirely by a human and one written entirely by an LLM

arms.name: Reviews classified human-written
arms.description: Existing human-classified reviews in the matched-paper corpus; review counts are not participant counts (p. 6, section 3.1; p. 13, Figure 11).

arms.name: Reviews classified LLM-generated
arms.description: Existing reviews classified as entirely LLM-generated by Pangram; model identities and actual reviewer workflows are unknown (p. 6, section 3.1).

participants.exclusions: Selection required a paper with one human-written and one LLM-generated review. Figure 11 additionally says the selected papers were on LLMs. These are corpus selection rules, not documented human participant exclusions (p. 6, section 3.1; p. 13, Figure 11).
participants.who: Scientific peer-review authors at ICLR 2026. The corpus is described as 18k reviews from 9k papers, with 9k human and 9k LLM reviews. These are output/paper counts, not people; no number of unique reviewers is stated (p. 6, section 3.1; p. 13, Figure 11). No eligible creativity/diversity outcome is extracted from this corpus, so there is no outcome n_units field to populate.
participants.locator: p. 6, section 3.1, Peer Reviews; p. 13, Figure 11

ai_tool.name_model: Generation models not stated; Pangram detects AI text; gpt-4o is the analysis judge
ai_tool.how_used: Real reviewer AI workflows were not observed. Pangram supplied AI-authorship classifications; gpt-4o extracted strength and weakness categories from review text (pp. 6-7, sections 3.1-3.2; pp. 44-45, section D.1). These analysis tools are not assigned writing treatments.

task.description: Scientific peer reviewing. The analysis concerns which scientific criteria reviews mention and the scores reviews assign to papers, not rated creativity of the reviews or a numerical across-review diversity measure (pp. 13-14, section 4.8; p. 46, Table 1).

studies.label: Initial protocol pilot (not a separate reported creativity-effect experiment)

assignment.what_was_assigned: A preliminary pilot tested the protocol and identified light/nonuse versus heavy-use behavior in the experimental condition. The pilot-specific allocation method and group counts are not reported, so the main experiment's randomization is not assumed for this sample.
assignment.quote: Before running the full experiment, we first conducted an initial pilot study

participants.exclusions: The pilot is reported as n = 8 and its data are described as analyzed to identify usage patterns; pilot exclusions and allocation counts are not stated. It precedes the n = 100 main study and is not added to the main sample (p. 5, section 3.1).
participants.who: Protocol-pilot participants; separate pilot recruitment, demographics, and residence are not stated in the pilot description (p. 5, section 3.1).
participants.quote: Analysis of this data revealed two distinct behaviors among participants in the experimental condition, with access to the LLM.

ai_tool.how_used: Some pilot participants had LLM access and differed in how much they used it; the pilot paragraph does not identify a separate model (p. 5, section 3.1).

task.description: Pilot of the essay-writing protocol, reported only to motivate classification of actual LLM-use patterns; no pilot output-based creativity/diversity result is reported (p. 5, section 3.1).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: S2 reuses the ArgRewrite-v2 sample of Kashefi et al. (2022), Argrewrite v.2: an annotated argumentative revisions corpus, DOI 10.1007/s10579-021-09567-z. S1 is presented as newly collected; no other paper sharing its participants is identified. S3 reuses existing conference-review records classified in the Pangram/Emi analysis, not a documented shared set of individual participants.
sample_overlap.quote: ArgRewrite-v2 (Kashefi et al., 2022) is a dataset of argumentative writing revisions collected from 86 university students.
sample_overlap.locator: pp. 5-6, section 3.1; p. 18, Kashefi et al. reference

company_involvement.description: Joel Z. Leibo, Max Kleiman-Weiner, and Natasha Jaques have Google DeepMind affiliations, and the copyright is Google DeepMind (p. 1). The acknowledgments name Toyota Research Institute, Character.AI, DoorDash, UW-Amazon Science Gift Hub, Sony Research Award Program, and UW-Tsukuba Amazon NVIDIA Cross Pacific AI Initiative among supporting/acknowledged organizations (p. 16); their individual operational roles are not specified.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, affiliations and copyright; p. 16, Acknowledgments

eligibility.reason: S1 explicitly randomizes people to LLM access versus no access (p. 4, section 3.1), reports a 100-person main sample (pp. 4-5, section 3.1; p. 26, Figure 12), and compares computed embeddings of their final essays across writers (p. 8, Figure 4b; p. 9, section 4.2). The writing task therefore supplies output-based diversity evidence, with AI available during production. Core eligibility is at study level: the plotted diversity result is descriptive and split by nonrandom actual usage, with no numerical full-arm randomized estimate or valid reported diversity SE for pooling. Criterion 3 is supported by the output embeddings, not by self-reported creativity. S2 is AI-versus-human context using a historical human sample; S3 is an observational corpus analysis without an eligible creativity/diversity outcome; S4 is a small protocol pilot without such an outcome.

one_line_finding: In the reported 100-person study, heavy LLM users' essays form a tighter semantic cluster and their self-rated creativity is 3.41 versus 3.95 in controls (p. 5, section 3.1; p. 8, Figure 4), but usage groups were not randomized.
open_questions: No numerical diversity effect or uncertainty is reported for S1 or S2. For causal estimation, obtain a participant-based diversity analysis comparing all assigned AI-access participants with all assigned controls; the published heavy/light-use comparisons do not retain randomization (pp. 4-5, section 3.1; pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and section 4.2).

The paper gives main N = 100 and assignment counts 45/55, but no complete-case counts for individual outcomes or account of exclusions. Figure 4a and Figure 6 print t(69); no subgroup/sample counts have been reverse-engineered from degrees of freedom or percentages (pp. 4-5, section 3.1; p. 8, Figure 4a; p. 10, Figure 6).

Confirm the Claude generation model: Figure 25 names Claude-3.5-Haiku (p. 34), whereas section I names Claude Haiku 4.5 (p. 61). MiniLM is named MiniLM-L6-v2 in the main text/section B.3 but MiniLM-L6-004 in appendix figure captions (p. 1, Figure 1; pp. 29-31, Figures 18-22).

Core eligibility treats the t-SNE comparison of output embeddings as figure-only diversity evidence. If the extraction gate requires a scalar diversity score rather than visual evidence of clustering, criterion 3 needs adjudication; this PDF supplies no such scalar score (pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and section 4.2).
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. The full markdown, including all essay examples through p. 95, was read, and PDF text was checked for the design, counts, quoted facts, and cited numerical results/figures. Four study entries comprise the three substantive studies described by the authors (p. 14, section 5) plus the explicitly reported n = 8 protocol pilot (p. 5); the pilot is not added to S1. Only the two output-based semantic-diversity outcome families are extracted. Self-reported creativity is not an output score: Figure 4a reports Human User 3.95, LLM-Influenced 3.83, LLM 3.41, with t(69) = 2.110, p = 0.0385 for heavy use versus control; the post-questionnaire asks How creative do you feel you were in writing the essay? (p. 8, Figure 4a and section 4.1; p. 24, section A.6). These self-report numbers do not establish criterion 3. Other measured variables are omitted because they do not score creativity or diversity: argumentative stance and argument categories (p. 10, Figure 6; p. 13, Figure 10b), parts-of-speech frequencies (p. 11, Figure 8), emotional word density (p. 12, Figure 9), and LIWC analytic language (p. 13, Figure 10a). The within-essay D1-to-D2 lexical JSD measures change from the same writer's original draft, not similarity across different writers (p. 7, section 3.2; pp. 10-11, section 4.4 and Figure 7); it is not coded as diversity. For context, Figure 6 reports neutral essays as 39.5% Human, 44.8% LLM-Influenced, and 66.7% LLM, with a printed 68.9% relative increase, t(69) = -2.439, p = 0.017; the section 4.3 prose gives p < 0.036 (p. 10). These are stance-category proportions, not a computed diversity index. S3 scores concern reviewed papers and which strengths/weaknesses their reviews mention; a Novelty category in Table 1 is not a novelty rating of the review itself (pp. 13-14, section 4.8; p. 46, Table 1). The Table 1 denominator is three times the review count, as its caption states, not people; its tests must not be treated as participant-level creativity precision. No after-AI creative task is reported. The code URL is explicitly given on pp. 1 and 8; no direct data-download URL is stated. No effect sizes or unprinted participant counts were calculated.
